gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a lab-measured brightness, contrast or power draw for any triple laptop screen extender. The nearest named measurements are for models that are over $400 or older: TechRadar measured 277.7 nits against a 300-nit rating and 15.2 W for three screens on the Aura Triple Boost 14 Pro, and Notebookcheck measured 185 cd/m², 247:1 contrast and 79% sRGB on a FOPO 12-inch triple. I found no named measurement for any candidate under $400.
standout_why: I read four of the pages ChatGPT got. UPERFECT's own triple-extender roundup (cited) gives only unattributed spec-sheet nits and sRGB figures and names no tester. The Office Journal says 'we research everything' and reports no measurements. Laptopbee reports one untested observation (15% battery in 33 minutes) with no method. PCWorld's KYY review (rank 7, not cited) weighed the KYY at about 6.5 lb against the 3.5 lb listed, so the 'weight runs over the spec' point is already in a result ChatGPT got. The TechRadar Aura and Notebookcheck FOPO readings are new, but they are for products that do not fit the question, and nothing measured covers the products ChatGPT recommended under $400. I could not open the Mobile Pixels Trio page (HTTP 429), Graded Picks (certificate error) or DeskFinds (HTTP 403).
decides: It does not decide the pick. No named reviewer or lab has measured the Trio 3 Pro, UPERFECT BE14BF, KEFEYA S2Pro, INVZI MagHub, Cevaton P7, Zumwalt S8 Pro or FOPO S1, S7, S9G or S11. The page can only warn that the two triple extenders measured near this price fell short of their claims: Aura 277.7 vs 300 nits (TechRadar), and KYY weighed about 6.5 lb vs 3.5 lb listed (PCWorld). It can also cite Macworld's Simon Jary: the Trio 3 Pro needs a power adapter for full brightness. The pick should rest on the video path (Alt Mode vs driver) and on price.
